title: Stress-directed growth of load-bearing structures

concept.text: The innovation is a nonliving structure that uses supplied feedstock to add strong material preferentially where mechanical stress indicates that reinforcement is needed. The added material must bond to the existing structure and carry load, increasing the failure capacity of a useful beam, panel or other structural member. The central advance is the integration of stress-directed placement, material growth and effective structural load transfer.

Bone-inspired adaptive materials provide a technical starting point: mechanical loading produces piezoelectric charges that promote mineral deposition, with greater deposition in more highly stressed regions. Existing examples therefore already demonstrate aspects of stress-directed reinforcement. The broader target is to extend that behavior to stronger, well-bonded structural material, useful growth rates and practical operating environments. Growth could reinforce an undamaged member beyond its original capacity as well as help restore capacity after damage.

significance.text: Successful structural growth would let a member increase its load capacity in response to the loads it actually experiences. Selective reinforcement would extend adaptation beyond a change in stiffness or the repair of an existing defect: the structure could acquire additional load-bearing material during service. The cited review identifies strengthening beyond original properties as a potential benefit of bone-inspired adaptation.

Potential downstream benefits include reducing unnecessary reserve mass, accommodating unexpected loading and recovering useful capacity after damage. These outcomes depend on growth occurring quickly enough, the new material remaining bonded and durable, and feedstock and energy reaching the required locations. A laboratory demonstration of increased failure load would establish an enabling capability; it would not by itself establish safe reductions in structural margins, reliable field recovery or net system-level mass savings.

Synthesis: the analogy with bone concerns load-responsive reinforcement. It does not establish that a synthetic structure would reproduce bone’s full biological regulation or maintain itself without resource delivery. Practical impact would depend on the complete growth system, including its supply equipment, operating constraints and inspection needs.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target breakthrough is feedstock-powered deposition of sufficiently strong, well-bonded material at stress-selected locations, fast enough to improve a useful member’s failure capacity. Deposition and adaptive reinforcement are already present in the reviewed research; the unresolved target is their integration into a more capable structural system. The supplied 2024 review documents limitations within the systems it covers, but does not establish that this broader capability remains absent across all approaches in November 2026.

The documented barriers include restricted material choices, limited mechanical properties, slow growth and dependence on liquid environments. The review describes polymer–mineral composites and reports that the adaptive behavior had not been demonstrated in metal or ceramic matrix materials within its scope. It identifies stronger substrates and reinforcing materials as research opportunities. Moving beyond liquid-electrolyte immersion would also expand the operating conditions available to a structural member.

Engineering synthesis: a convincing system must connect the stress response to useful reinforcement rather than merely accumulate material. It must deliver feedstock to stressed regions, form a durable interface, and transfer load through the deposit without the interface becoming the limiting weakness. Growth must also occur on a timescale relevant to the loading and damage being addressed. These are integrated engineering requirements inferred from the structural target, rather than separately demonstrated solutions in the supplied record.

current_state.text: Grant Kitchen, Bohan Sun and Sung Hoon Kang’s 2024 review, “Bone-inspired dynamically adaptive materials: Current efforts and future opportunities,” describes systems in which loading and piezoelectric effects promote localized mineral deposition. Because charge magnitude depends on loading, new material preferentially forms in regions experiencing higher stress. This establishes a technical basis for stress-directed material addition, while leaving the stronger integrated structural target open.

For the systems it surveys, the review reports elastic moduli of approximately 10–100 MPa and mineral growth rates on the order of 10–100 micrometres per day. Elastic modulus measures stiffness; these values are not measurements of failure strength or allowable working stress and cannot be used to show that the proposed 20 MPa working-stress benchmark has been met. The growth-rate figures likewise do not alone establish how quickly a useful member could gain a specified amount of failure capacity.

The reviewed examples use polymer–mineral composites immersed in liquid electrolyte. Immersion constrains deployment and restricts temperature to conditions in which the electrolyte remains liquid. The review does not demonstrate a metal-class structural member doubling its failure load in air. Its discussion of stronger materials and broader operating conditions describes future opportunities, rather than achieved performance.

The supplied evidence review reports verified, complete article text, and the source index records untruncated HTML and PDF extractions without reported extraction issues. The interpretation here relies on the supplied review’s account of the text and does not depend on inspection of figure images. No freshness search was supplied to establish subsequent progress through November 1, 2026; retrieving the 2024 article in November 2026 does not update its scientific coverage. This evidence supports a dated account of demonstrated mechanisms and limitations, rather than a verified present-day absence of the broader capability.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a nonliving beam or panel in laboratory air with a defined feedstock and repeatable cyclic loading. Show that material grows preferentially in highly stressed regions and that the added material bonds to the member and transfers load. Specify the loading history, feedstock delivery arrangement, growth conditions and methods used to establish spatial selectivity and load transfer.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed quantitative benchmark: use matched specimen cohorts and independent destructive testing to demonstrate at least twice the failure load of otherwise matched controls in which growth is disabled. Under a specified service load, demonstrate at least 20 MPa working stress in the grown load path, with the stress definition, measurement or inference method, and uncertainty stated explicitly. Doubling failure load and reaching 20 MPa are proposed choices, not established standards, reported achievements or evidence of metal-class performance.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed quantitative benchmark

completion_criteria.text: Proposed damage test: introduce a defined, controlled damage event in a separate specimen cohort, then repeat the growth-and-testing protocol against matched damaged specimens with growth disabled. Separate cohorts are needed because measuring ultimate failure load destroys the specimen. Report both improvement relative to damaged controls and capacity relative to an undamaged baseline, so that reinforcement after damage is distinguished from full recovery of original capacity.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed damage test

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: report specimen variability, growth duration, feedstock consumption, added mass, energy use and uncertainty, and reproduce the result across independently prepared specimens. Any claim that growth is fast enough for service must include a response-time requirement tied to the relevant load or damage timescale; recording elapsed time alone is insufficient. Testing would establish performance for the demonstrated materials, geometries, loads and environments. Broader applicability would require further validation, including durability and interface performance, and finite tests would not establish universal adaptation.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: MEC-04, “Ambient fatigue immunity in bulk structural metals,” concerns resistance to fatigue damage. MEC-10 instead concerns adding material in response to stress to increase or restore load capacity. The approaches could complement each other, but stress-directed growth would not itself establish fatigue immunity. Full MEC-04 details were not supplied, so this comparison is limited to its title and the supplied characterization of crack resistance.

Roster-based comparison: MEC-05, “Programmable solids that become different load-bearing mechanisms,” concerns changing how a solid functions mechanically; the supplied research characterizes that change as reversible. MEC-10 concerns feedstock addition and growth of a bonded load path. A structure could potentially combine these capabilities, but neither establishes the other. The full MEC-05 concept was not supplied.

Stress-directed growth overlaps with self-healing when new material repairs damage. Its scope also includes reinforcing an initially undamaged structure beyond its original capacity. Repair and strengthening are therefore related outcomes, with different comparisons needed to establish each one.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-07, “Bulk structural solids at a large fraction of ideal strength,” concerns the strength of structural material itself, whereas MEC-10 concerns where material is added and how it contributes to a member’s capacity. MEC-06, “Macroscopic atomically precise mechanosynthesis,” concerns fabrication precision, which stress-directed growth does not inherently require. MEC-09, “Mechanical self-replication of a production cell from feedstock,” also involves feedstock-driven construction, but reinforcing an existing member is distinct from reproducing a production system.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-11, “Transferable prediction of wear and component life,” and MEC-12, “Predictive mechanics of real, evolving surface contacts,” could help evaluate lifetime and changing interfaces in an adaptive structure. They concern predictive capabilities, whereas MEC-10 concerns a physical capacity to grow reinforcement. These possible connections are inferred from the supplied titles and do not establish technical dependencies.

change_log.change: Preserved MEC-10’s identity while defining the target as integrated stress-directed deposition, bonding and increased structural failure capacity.
change_log.reason: Existing adaptive reinforcement means that deposition or strengthening alone cannot accurately be described as wholly missing.

change_log.change: Dated the demonstrated mechanisms and limitations to the supplied 2024 review and retained uncertainty about subsequent progress.
change_log.reason: The empty freshness record cannot establish field-wide absence of the capability in November 2026.

change_log.change: Integrated the reported 10–100 MPa elastic-modulus range and 10–100 micrometres-per-day mineral growth rate.
change_log.reason: These quantitative details explain the documented limitations, while distinguishing stiffness from strength prevents an invalid comparison with the proposed working-stress benchmark.

change_log.change: Made reserve-mass reduction, damage recovery and field benefits explicitly conditional on speed, bonding, durability, resource supply and validated safety.
change_log.reason: A laboratory capacity gain would establish an enabling capability without proving those downstream benefits.

change_log.change: Revised the proposed demonstration to use matched cohorts, disabled-growth controls, independent destructive testing and explicit tests of stress selectivity and load transfer.
change_log.reason: Failure testing is destructive, and increased capacity alone does not establish that growth followed stress or that the deposit formed a useful bonded load path.

change_log.change: Separated the damaged-specimen experiment and clarified recovery comparisons, resource accounting and service-relevant timing.
change_log.reason: The original protocol left repetition after destructive testing ambiguous and recorded time without defining a sufficient response rate.

change_log.change: Retained doubling failure load and 20 MPa working stress as proposed benchmarks, with explicit limits on their interpretation.
change_log.reason: Neither number is a published completion standard, demonstrated result or sufficient basis for a metal-class performance claim.

change_log.change: Expanded related-concept distinctions and preserved the limits of title-based comparisons.
change_log.reason: The roster supports useful conceptual connections, but full records for the other innovations were not supplied.

change_log.change: Preserved extraction completeness and figure-inspection limitations without implying independent document inspection.
change_log.reason: The supplied review supports text-based conclusions; it does not authorize claims based on uninspected images or a new source assessment.

unresolved_issues: Whether any approach achieved the broader structural target after the 2024 review remains unresolved; no freshness search was supplied through November 1, 2026.
The proposed benchmark has no numerical growth-time requirement. A service application and its loading or damage timescale must be specified before response speed can be judged sufficient.
The specimen geometry, material system, feedstock, damage protocol, working-stress definition and uncertainty requirements remain to be specified for an executable demonstration.
The supplied record does not establish whether air operation, adequate bonding, the proposed capacity gain and durable performance can be achieved together in one system.
Net reserve-mass savings, long-term reliability and safe deployment remain conditional system-level questions beyond the proposed laboratory demonstration.
Detailed overlap with MEC-04, MEC-05 and the other related roster entries remains limited by the absence of their full concept records.
